answer_text:
# 🦴 Bones of the Head (Human Skull)

The human skull is generally considered to consist of **22 bones** — **8 cranial bones** and **14 facial skeleton bones**. Some sources also include the hyoid bone and the three ossicles of the middle ear (malleus, incus, and stapes), bringing the total to 29 bones.

The skull is divided into two regions: the **neurocranium** (which protects the brain) and the **viscerocranium** (which forms the face).

---

## 🧠 Part 1: The Neurocranium (Braincase) — 8 Bones

The cranium is the skeletal structure of the head that supports the face and protects the brain. It is subdivided into the **facial bones** and the **brain case (cranial vault)**.

The cranium is composed of **8 cranial bones**: the **frontal bone**, a **parietal bone** on each side, a **temporal bone** on each side, the **occipital bone**, the **ethmoid bone**, and the **sphenoid bone**.

| Bone | Description |
|---|---|
| **Frontal Bone** (×1) | A single, seamless bone that gives your forehead its structure. |
| **Parietal Bones** (×2) | Form the sides and uppermost portion of the dome of the cranium. |
| **Temporal Bones** (×2) | Form the lower lateral sides of the skull. They subdivide into petrous, squamous, zygomatic, and mastoid parts; the petrous portion houses the inner ear. |
| **Occipital Bone** (×1) | Forms the base of the cranium and has a central opening (foramen magnum) to admit the spinal cord. |
| **Sphenoid Bone** (×1) | A single bone below and in front of the brain, behind the bones making up the face. It also forms part of the lower rear of the eye sockets. |
| **Ethmoid Bone** (×1) | Forms part of the cranial floor. It also forms part of the nasal cavity and eye sockets. |

---

## 😊 Part 2: The Facial Skeleton (Viscerocranium) — 14 Bones

The facial skeleton supports the soft tissues of the face. It consists of **14 bones**, which fuse to house the orbits of the eyes, the nasal and oral cavities, and the sinuses.

The 14 bones of the facial skeleton are: the **vomer**, two **inferior nasal conchae**, two **nasal bones**, two **maxilla**, the **mandible**, two **palatine bones**, two **zygomatic bones**, and two **lacrimal bones**.

| Bone | Description |
|---|---|
| **Mandible** (×1) | Makes up the lower jaw. It is the **only bone of the skull that moves**. |
| **Maxilla** (×2) | One on the left and one on the right, they form the top jaw and anchor the upper teeth. |
| **Zygomatic Bones** (×2) | The cheekbones, which join with the temporal and maxillary bones to form the zygomatic arch below the eye socket. |
| **Nasal Bones** (×2) | Form the bridge of the nose. |
| **Palatine Bones** (×2) | Form the roof of the mouth and help to form the mouth cavity. |
| **Lacrimal Bones** (×2) | The smallest bones of the face, located in the inner wall of the eye socket. |
| **Inferior Nasal Conchae** (×2) | Scroll-like bones inside the nasal cavity that help with airflow. |
| **Vomer** (×1) | Helps form the nasal cavity. It forms the lower part of the nasal septum. |

---

## 🔗 Sutures (Joints Between the Bones)

Sutures are a type of fibrous joint unique to the skull. They are immovable and fuse completely around the age of 20. The main sutures are:

- **Coronal suture** – fuses the frontal bone with the two parietal bones.
- **Sagittal suture** – fuses both parietal bones to each other.
- **Lambdoid suture** – fuses the occipital bone to the two parietal bones.

---

## 👶 In Infants

In neonates, the incompletely fused suture joints give rise to membranous gaps between the bones, known as **fontanelles**. The two major ones are the **frontal fontanelle** (at the junction of the coronal and sagittal sutures) and the **occipital fontanelle** (at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures).
